groups.name: High-volume base metals
groups.tagline: Defined by scale, not monopoly leverage.
groups.body:
Every mineral here is consumed in hundreds of thousands to millions of tonnes annually. Supply is comparatively diffuse: no single country monopolises mining, and while China dominates refining for some, none approaches the leverage it holds over rare earths. The binding risk is sheer volume: these minerals power construction, energy, transport, and agriculture so broadly that a sustained shortfall would transmit immediately across the entire economy.

Cobalt and lithium sit here despite their high import dependence and price volatility because their defining feature is the same as the others: the risk arises from the scale of demand, not from a chokepoint that one supplier controls. Potash and phosphorus, the two primary plant nutrients that have to be mined rather than made, sit here for the same reason: India's exposure is the sheer tonnage it imports for fertiliser. The policy question for this group is not who controls them but whether India has sufficient industrial processing capacity and strategic reserves to absorb a price spike or temporary disruption.
policy: Aggressively scale up midstream processing infrastructure: target capital-intensive midstream, specifically chemical refining, smelting and precursor manufacturing. Incentivise KABIL and private conglomerates to move beyond upstream mining exploration and invest in overseas processing facilities within resource-rich, friendly nations.
Scale secondary scrap infrastructure and enforce strict extended producer responsibility (EPR) targets.

groups.name: Heavy rare earths
groups.body: This is the tightest group in the dataset, and the one where India's exposure is most acute and its options fewest. Every rare earth here scores at or near the maximum on three vectors simultaneously: refining concentration, reserve concentration, and extraction complexity. Reserves are locked in ion-adsorption clay deposits in southern China and Myanmar. The refining process, multi-stage solvent extraction of chemically near-identical elements, requires capability that no Indian facility has at commercial scale; outside China, only Lynas's plant in Malaysia has begun producing separated heavy rare earths commercially (from May 2025). Substitution is either technically impossible or requires a fundamental product redesign that takes years. China's monopoly in these minerals is the hardest to dent in the immediate term. The April 2025 export controls caused Western market prices to triple within weeks, and Indian automotive and EV manufacturers were among the first firms denied licenses. We did an explainer and state-of-the-market analysis on rare-earth-free EV motors. Check it out here.
policy: Aggressively execute the Sintered Rare Earth Permanent Magnet (REPM) scheme.
Pursue joint stockpiling through international partnerships.
Ultimately, the way out may be to make these minerals obsolete, specifically via Synchronous Reluctance Motors (SynRM) and induction motors that eliminate rare-earth permanent magnets entirely.

groups.name: Closed-loop high-value minerals
groups.tagline: High recycling rates and high-value applications define this group.
groups.body:
The commonality in this group lies in high recycling. Reserves for minerals here tend to be concentrated, but are also long-lived relative to demand. This group largely consists of platinum group elements (PGEs) alongside indium, beryllium, hafnium and tantalum, all of which follow similar characterisations: technically demanding to produce, expensive, and consumed in small volumes for high-value applications.

Because they are expensive and widely deployed in industrial catalysts, electronics, and medical devices, secondary recovery is commercially viable in a way it is not for cheaper, more widely dispersed minerals. This does not make them without risk, reserves are concentrated and extraction barriers are high, but the closed-loop dynamic gives the supply chain a resilience that the heavy rare earths group lacks entirely. The intervention point for this group is maintaining and deepening recycling infrastructure rather than upstream mining investment.
policy: Double down on recycling. India's transition to Bharat Stage VI (BS-VI) emission standards means a massive, rapidly maturing pool of platinum, palladium and rhodium riding inside vehicle catalytic converters. The National Green Hydrogen Mission also relies heavily on Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolyzers, which need some of these minerals.
Streamline collection networks through cross-border B2B "strategic scrap" exchange, introduce specific EPR credits, and expand recycling facilities.

groups.name: Wait and Watch
groups.tagline: High concentration. Low volatility. The monopoly not being exercised.
groups.body:
This group is a direct corrective to the assumption that concentration automatically signals danger. Every member here is dominated by a single country or producer, yet this group records the lowest price volatility and weakest demand growth of any of the six. The monopoly is real; it is simply not being exercised, at least not yet.

The reasons differ by mineral. Brazil's CBMM manages niobium supply with deliberate discipline, holding prices stable at around $26/kg over years. Lanthanum and cerium come out of the ground mainly as by-products of mining the more valuable neodymium, so they pile up in oversupply whether or not anyone needs them. Vanadium prices fell 27% in 2024 on weak Chinese steel demand. Europium has so few uses left that almost no one buys it. For policy, what matters is that these minerals could become dangerous if geopolitics shift, but this is not happening currently. Monitoring rather than urgent intervention may be the appropriate posture.
policy: Leverage early-warning tools to track global shifts, such as Chinese real-estate/steel demand (for vanadium) or production shifts at Brazil's CBMM (for niobium), and implement a "just-in-time" blueprint: if China suddenly weaponises its vanadium or lanthanum supply, a pre-drafted policy automatically triggers, such as fast-tracked waivers for steel-slag processing or immediate customs-duty draw-backs for alternative imports.
Steel-slag harvesting: for vanadium, mandate that domestic steel giants (like SAIL or JSW) monitor and catalogue the vanadium content in their industrial slag.

Because Brazil's CBMM deliberately keeps niobium prices stable ($26/kg) to protect market share, India's private infrastructure and defence conglomerates should sign long-term, fixed-price offtake agreements, and the government could use bilateral diplomacy to secure "preferred buyer" status. This locks in supply via state-to-state paperwork rather than capital-heavy asset acquisition.

groups.name: A widening processing chokepoint
groups.tagline: Reserves are everywhere; the processing chokepoint is widening.
groups.body:
This group is characterised by extreme refining concentration paired with rapid demand growth and a diversified reserve base. The reserves are well distributed across multiple countries, so geology is not the constraint. Demand is large and accelerating, driven by EV batteries, solar panels, and semiconductor fabs. Several members score at the maximum on the growth vector. The midstream gap is widening.

Graphite: China controls 90% of battery-grade processing while India targets 150 GW of new battery capacity. Silicon: prices spiked 273% in 2022 when Chinese power rationing shut domestic plants, then collapsed equally fast. Neodymium and praseodymium: every EV motor and wind turbine generator depends on them, and the April 2025 export controls hit this supply chain directly. Gallium: India is the world's fifth-largest bauxite producer but does not yet recover gallium (a demonstration plant at NALCO's Damanjodi refinery broke ground in November 2025). The raw resource is globally available in each case; the processing chokepoint is the problem, and it is actively widening.
policy: Leverage international partnerships for processing and recycling capacities.

groups.name: Diffused-risk and by-product minerals
groups.tagline: No single sharp bottleneck; mostly mined as by-products.
groups.body:
These are the least concentrated minerals supply-wise, and also have the lowest scores on the end-use applications vector. The profile that holds them together is the absence of any extreme: demand is moderate, supply concentration is low to middling, reserves are adequate, and extraction is comparatively undemanding. None presents a single sharp bottleneck that would justify urgent strategic intervention.

Some minerals in this group do have isolated extreme features: antimony, germanium and tellurium have high price volatility scores, and rhenium has no substitute in fighter engine superalloys, but they still share the defining feature of low overall constraint. Interestingly, a majority are mined as by-products of other major minerals: bismuth, germanium, and cadmium are by-products of lead and zinc; selenium, tellurium and rhenium are by-products of copper. Their availability is governed less by dedicated supply chains than by the economics of the host metals they accompany.
policy: Tighten "companionability reporting" for base-metal miners to log concentrations of bismuth, germanium and cadmium in their zinc/lead ores, and selenium, tellurium and rhenium in their copper ores.

Introduce a "royalty-offset credit" system: if a domestic zinc smelter invests its own capital to install advanced hydrometallurgical circuits to isolate germanium or bismuth, the government offers a matching discount on its primary zinc mining royalties. Processing and recycling of these minerals should also feature in India's international partnerships to insulate against price volatility.
Build joint "micro-reserves" for select minerals like rhenium.

groups.name: Outlier
groups.tagline: Not a commercial mineral. A genuine singleton.
groups.body: When the clustering separates minerals more finely, promethium is the only element that splits off entirely on its own. Promethium is not a commercial mineral. It is radioactive, has no stable isotope, does not occur naturally in extractable quantities, and is produced in gram-scale quantities as a fission by-product in nuclear reactors. The US Department of Energy's Isotope Program is the sole global commercial supplier. There is no commodity market, no price index, and no supply chain in the conventional sense. Its presence on India's critical minerals list, and on most others, appears to be an artefact of completeness.

vectors.name: Current Global Demand
vectors.what: Absolute annual global consumption. Determines the scale of any feasible intervention.

vectors.name: Projected Demand Growth to 2030
vectors.what: Trajectory of demand, by compound annual growth rate (CAGR). Signals where future bottlenecks form.

vectors.name: End-use Applications
vectors.what: How many critical sectors depend on the mineral, and how strategic those sectors are. A sectoral additive score (max 7) plus a breadth bonus (max 3).

sub.name: Sectoral score
sub.note: Defence +1.5, Energy/Grid +1.5, Agriculture +1.5, Semiconductors +1, Transport/EV +1, Healthcare +1, Construction +0.5; a minor use in a sector earns +0.5

sub.name: Breadth bonus
sub.note: +0.5 per additional qualifying sector beyond the first, up to +3 at seven sectors

vectors.name: Supplier Concentration
vectors.what: How concentrated supply is, scored separately for mining and refining because for many minerals the ore is distributed but the processing is monopolised. Each subscore uses the largest single country's share of global output.

vectors.name: Global Reserves
vectors.what: Two questions: how long reserves last at current consumption, and how geographically concentrated they are.

vectors.name: Substitutability & Recyclability
vectors.what: The two exits from a supply squeeze: replacing the mineral, or recovering it from secondary sources. Scored independently.

sub.name: Substitutability
sub.note: 1: drop-in substitute >20% of market; 5: no substitute at any cost

vectors.name: Extraction & Refining Complexity
vectors.what: Technical difficulty of production, a barrier to entry that determines how contestable a concentration is.

bands.label: Simple, widely accessible (standard mining + physical separation)
Highly complex (near-identical element separation; <10–15 facilities worldwide)

vectors.name: Upcoming Projects
vectors.what: Whether a current bottleneck is temporary or durable, judged by the project pipeline.

bands.label: Strong pipeline (>20% new supply, output 2–3 yrs)
No pipeline; structural barrier to scaling

vectors.name: India's Position
vectors.what: India-specific: how dependent on imports, and how far India has moved to secure the mineral.

sub.name: Strategic posture
sub.note: 1: secured (offtakes/equity/processing); 3: intent declared only; 5: no awareness

vectors.name: Price Volatility
vectors.what: How violently the price has moved, independent of supply concentration. A cost to investment planning in its own right.

bands.note: Already > 20% market share; commercially deployed by multiple manufacturers

bands.note: Industry can adapt within 1–2 years; at least one major manufacturer has deployed

bands.label: Significant trade-offs (> 50% cost premium)
bands.note: 3–5 year adaptation; only at pilot scale or limited commercial use

bands.note: No commercial-scale alternative; switching requires fundamental product redesign

bands.note: Proven technology for high-concentration scrap; end-of-life limited by logistics

bands.note: Operating mines and/or refineries at commercial scale

bands.label: 40–60% domestic
bands.note: Mostly self-sufficient; imports supplement but don't define supply

bands.label: 20–40% domestic

bands.label: < 20% domestic
bands.note: Marginal production; some resources or operations but token relative to demand

bands.label: Zero domestic production
bands.note: 100% import-dependent

bands.label: Active secured position
bands.note: Binding offtakes, equity stakes in foreign assets, or operational JVs delivering material

bands.label: Concrete plans in motion
bands.note: Exploration blocks auctioned; MOUs/framework agreements signed; KABIL active due diligence; output 3–7 yrs

bands.label: Strategic intent declared
bands.note: On official critical minerals list; mentioned in policy documents; no specific projects or agreements yet

bands.label: Passive awareness
bands.note: Acknowledged as important; no KABIL mandate, no exploration blocks, no foreign outreach

bands.label: No awareness or relevance
bands.note: Not identified as strategic; India is a passive importer of finished goods

bands.label: Stable (within ± 20% over 5 yrs)
bands.note: Dominated by long-term contracts; often managed by a single producer; no exchange trading

bands.label: Low (± 20–50%)
bands.note: Gradual movements driven by transparent factors; mix of contract and spot; liquid market

bands.label: Moderate (± 50–100%)
bands.note: At least one notable spike or correction; partially opaque market; active procurement management needed

bands.label: High (> ± 100%)
bands.note: Thin and opaque market; sensitive to single-actor decisions; genuine procurement uncertainty

bands.label: Extreme (> 200% or market breakdown)
bands.note: Export bans or weaponised supply; price can double overnight; supply cannot be reliably secured

capability.nextMove: Keep the strategic chain at BARC and draw on the beryl stockpile; for industry, start with beryllium-copper alloy made from imported master alloy.
capability.has: BARC's beryllium plant at Vashi, Navi Mumbai, at work since 1982; 4,250 t of beryl stockpiled by the Atomic Minerals Directorate; beryl deposits in five states. Beryllium is a prescribed substance under the Atomic Energy Act, and there is no commercial production.

capability.step: Indium recovery from zinc residues and scrap
capability.nextMove: Assay Hindustan Zinc's residues for indium, and pilot CSIR-NML's recovery of indium from scrap display panels.
capability.has: Large zinc smelters with no indium circuit (IBM records no production). CSIR-NML has a laboratory process that recovers about 97% of the indium from scrap LCD panels; the Nuclear Fuel Complex developed high-purity indium and passed the technology to industry.

capability.nextMove: Prove up the niobium found with rare earths in Gujarat and Rajasthan, and scale the Nuclear Fuel Complex's niobium line.
capability.has: 142,200 t of niobium oxide in hard-rock rare-earth deposits of Gujarat and Rajasthan (Atomic Minerals Directorate); auctioned blocks in Rajasthan; the Nuclear Fuel Complex makes reactor-grade and superconductor-grade niobium, and VSSC's 3 t/yr niobium thermit facility there serves the space programme.

capability.nextMove: Scale sponge beyond 1,000 t/yr and qualify aerospace grades.
capability.has: Mineral-sands mining and separation (IREL, KMML); KMML's chloride-route TiCl4; a 500 t/yr sponge plant (DMRL process, funded by ISRO) with expansion to 1,000 t under way.

capability.nextMove: Synthetic graphite anode for non-China cell makers; secure premium coke.
capability.has: Large electrode makers with graphitisation know-how (HEG 100 kt, Graphite India 80 kt); TACC's 20 kt/yr anode plant near Indore; Epsilon's planned 100 kt/yr at Bellary; GFCL is setting up an anode facility.

capability.nextMove: Publish and scale Hindalco's copper telluride recovery at Dahej, add a circuit at Kutch Copper, and refine to 5N for cadmium telluride.
capability.has: Hindalco's process at Dahej recovers tellurium from slime leachate as copper telluride (no volumes published); Kutch Copper's slime; high-purity tellurium at the Nuclear Fuel Complex; First Solar's 3.3 GW plant as a buyer.

capability.nextMove: Win customer approvals and fill the new carbonate plant, lock in celestite supply, then move into ferrite magnets.
capability.has: Vishnu Chemicals, the first maker of strontium carbonate in India: a plant at Visakhapatnam with about 10,000 t/yr of operating capacity, expandable to 17,000, commercialised in 2025. Celestite ore is imported, now free of customs duty.

capability.nextMove: Silicon metal from ferrosilicon know-how, then polysilicon under the planned MNRE scheme.
capability.has: Ferroalloy furnace know-how; 213 GW of module and 32 GW of cell capacity as a captive market; integrated PLI awards to Indosol and Reliance.

capability.nextMove: Chemical (APT) recycling so scrap is processed at home; mine later.
capability.has: Sandvik's carbide-recycling plant at Chiplun; HZL's tungsten block; a large tooling industry that generates scrap.

capability.nextMove: Turn Hindustan Zinc's by-product stream into metal and trioxide at scale; tie up concentrate for the smelters India already runs.
capability.has: Smelters that run on imported ore and concentrate (6,460 t in 2022-23) and export metal; Hindustan Zinc, which recovers antimony from smelter dust and slag as a by-product; high-purity antimony and antimony trioxide at the Nuclear Fuel Complex.

capability.nextMove: Commercial hafnium from NFC's raffinate; secure zircon supply.
capability.has: NFC's complete nuclear zirconium chain (separation, sponge, Zircaloy). Its Zr-Hf separation leaves hafnium raffinate: ~12-25 t/yr of hafnium (our estimate). C-MET makes hafnium sponge for ISRO.

capability.nextMove: Recover bismuth where lead and zinc are already smelted; Hindustan Zinc says it is building that capability.
capability.has: Bismuth occurs in Hindustan Zinc's Rajpura-Dariba lead-zinc deposit, and the company is developing in-house extraction of bismuth and other minor metals from smelter waste. The Nuclear Fuel Complex makes high-purity bismuth in small lots. No commercial production.

capability.nextMove: Scale refining of imported hydroxide and black mass into battery-grade cobalt sulphate.
capability.has: Hydrometallurgical refining at Nicomet and Rubamin on imported intermediates and scrap; Rubamin also recovers cobalt from spent catalysts; CSIR-IMMT has a superalloy-scrap process; seabed nodule contracts.

capability.nextMove: Secure concentrate; treat slime fully for tellurium, selenium and PGMs, with commercial tellurium circuits at Dahej and Kutch and 5N purification for CdTe.
capability.has: Three large smelter-refiners (Hindalco Dahej, Kutch Copper at 0.5 Mt/yr, Vedanta Silvassa) with slime circuits for precious metals and selenium; Hindalco lists CSIR-IMMT's tellurium process (85-90% recovery) as implemented. India's copper carries ~25-45 t/yr of tellurium (our estimate).

capability.nextMove: Recover germanium at Hindustan Zinc's planned tailings plant, and scale DRDO's germanium crystal growth for infrared optics.
capability.has: Hindustan Zinc's 10 Mt/yr tailings reprocessing plant at Rampura Agucha (approved 2025) is meant to recover zinc and critical minerals including germanium; DRDO's Solid State Physics Laboratory grows optical-grade germanium crystals and lens blanks.

capability.step: Rhenium from copper smelting and scrap
capability.nextMove: Capture the rhenium that arrives in imported concentrates, put at 1.5 to 2 t a year, and recover it from spent reforming catalysts and superalloy scrap.
capability.has: No recovery (IBM records no production). A 2023 study estimates that the concentrates India processes carry 1.5 to 2 t of recoverable rhenium a year, none of it captured. Hindustan Platinum treats spent catalysts, but the metals it reports recovering do not include rhenium.

capability.nextMove: Scale the Nuclear Fuel Complex's tantalum line on stockpiled and imported concentrate, and recover tantalum from capacitor scrap.
capability.has: The Nuclear Fuel Complex makes tantalum pentoxide and tantalum metal and developed capacitor-grade powder and anodes; VSSC's niobium facility there processes columbite-tantalite by solvent extraction; the Atomic Minerals Directorate holds 149 t of columbite-tantalite. No commercial mining (IBM).

capability.nextMove: Two tracks: keep fertiliser supply secure through the overseas acid plants and long-term offtakes; add battery-grade purified acid and iron phosphate for LFP.
capability.has: Fertiliser acid plants at home (IFFCO, PPL, Coromandel) and co-owned plants abroad: IMACID in Morocco (Chambal with OCP, expanding from 500 to 700 kt/yr of acid) and JIFCO in Jordan (IFFCO with JPMC); five-year Ma'aden deals for 3.1 Mt/yr of DAP; Sudeep's pharma-to-battery iron phosphate; Himadri and GFCL LFP cathode projects.

capability.nextMove: Prove solution mining of Rajasthan potash; scale brine-based SOP.
capability.has: Archean's brine-based SOP; Rajasthan's ~236 Mt of resources and an MECL-RSMML solution-mining study; a large fertiliser-blending industry.

capability.nextMove: Commercial gallium circuits at the big refineries, with 6N refining.
capability.has: 8.2 Mt/yr of alumina refining (~80 t/yr of gallium in the liquor at China's yield, our estimate); the NALCO-HWB/BARC ion-exchange demo plant; C-MET's 6N purification; Indian resin makers.

capability.nextMove: Keep refinery and hydroprocessing catalysts in India for recovery; take in Gulf catalysts as feed.
capability.has: Rubamin processes ~20,000 t/yr of spent catalyst and recovers ~1,500 t/yr of molybdenum; India's ~249 Mt/yr of refining is a steady catalyst stream.

capability.nextMove: Work the Chhattisgarh deposits at scale and recover tin from solder and tinplate scrap.
capability.has: Small mine output in Dantewada, Chhattisgarh (45 t of concentrate in 2022-23) and one smelter at Jagdalpur (17 t of metal); 103,757 t of contained tin in resources, 64% of the ore in Haryana; a tin block auctioned in Chhattisgarh.

capability.nextMove: Near term: refine imported mixed hydroxide into sulphate. Long term: test Sukinda overburden at pilot scale.
capability.has: Small refining (Nicomet; Hindustan Copper's nickel sulphate); CSIR-IMMT's 10 t/day proving plant for Sukinda overburden; ferroalloy furnace know-how close to RKEF; seabed nodules (1.14% Ni).

capability.step: Vanadium from sludge, slag and refinery residues
capability.nextMove: Recover vanadium from what India already processes: Bayer sludge at alumina refineries, steel slag, refinery petcoke and spent catalysts.
capability.has: Vanadium sludge at alumina refineries (BALCO 6 to 10% V2O5, Hindalco Renukoot 8.2%); recovery processes at Vedanta Lanjigarh, NALCO (lab) and Reliance (gasifier slag, lab to pilot); 839 t of ferro-vanadium made in 2022-23.

capability.nextMove: Mid-stream chemicals first: electrolyte salts and electrolytes, sold to non-China cell makers. Then conversion of imported spodumene.
capability.has: No domestic mine. Lohum refines black mass and spodumene and now mines in Zimbabwe. GFCL makes LiPF6 within a Rs 6,000 crore battery-chemicals programme. Neogen is building 5,500 t/yr of electrolyte salts and 32,000 t/yr of electrolyte.

capability.nextMove: Recover Tb from magnet scrap; use grain-boundary diffusion to cut Tb per magnet; heavy-REE separation later.
capability.has: Same base as dysprosium: IREL's pilot separation, magnet recovery at Bhopal, Neyveli ash and new magnet makers.

capability.nextMove: Self-supply oxide for coatings and lasers; test Neyveli ash.
capability.has: IREL's yttrium oxide; NLC-BARC fly-ash pilot (Neyveli ash ~300 mg/kg of Y).

capability.nextMove: Recover Dy from magnet scrap and test Neyveli ash; build heavy-REE separation once feed is secured.
capability.has: IREL's separation know-how (light REEs commercial, heavy ones at pilot scale); a facility at Bhopal that recovers REEs from end-of-life magnets; Neyveli ash and the NLC-BARC pilot; magnet makers coming under the Rs 7,280 crore scheme.

capability.nextMove: Scale C-MET's hafnium sponge pilot on the Nuclear Fuel Complex's raffinate, and add crystal-bar refining.
capability.has: The Nuclear Fuel Complex strips hafnium from zirconium for reactor tubes; IREL has made 99% hafnium oxide from that raffinate; C-MET and VSSC run a 320 kg/yr sponge pilot.

capability.nextMove: Fill Kutch Copper's 150 t/yr selenium capacity and add high-purity refining; India still imports more than it makes.
capability.has: About 90 t refined in 2025 from anode slime at Hindalco Dahej and Kutch Copper; 150 t/yr of capacity at Kutch Copper; Hindustan Copper's Ghatsila plant, which last reported selenium in 2006-07.

capability.nextMove: Turn surplus lanthanum into cracking-catalyst additives for India's refineries.
capability.has: IREL separates lanthanum oxide of over 99% purity at Aluva; Toyotsu refines lanthanum at Visakhapatnam. IBM lists lanthanum among the rare earths India has in surplus, and IREL calls the home market for its rare-earth products almost non-existent.

capability.nextMove: Scale the cadmium recovery that Hindustan Zinc and Runaya restarted in FY2026, then add high-purity refining for solar and nuclear use.
capability.has: 913 t/yr of installed recovery capacity at zinc smelters (Chanderiya 468, Debari 250; Vizag and Binani suspended). Hindustan Zinc made cadmium products again in FY2026 by refining purification cake with Runaya, which is adding cadmium capacity in Rajasthan.

capability.nextMove: Use the surplus: make polishing powder and catalyst-grade ceria in India from IREL and Toyotsu oxide.
capability.has: IREL separates cerium oxide of over 99% purity at Aluva and is India's only monazite processor; Toyotsu refines cerium at Visakhapatnam. IBM lists cerium among the rare earths India has in surplus, and IREL calls the home market for its rare-earth products almost non-existent.

capability.nextMove: Build recovery only with an anchor buyer (aerospace alloys, fuel cells).
capability.has: NALCO's fly-ash pilot with CSIR-IMMT; red mud at the alumina refineries; CSIR-NML projects on scandium from tin slag and Al-Sc alloys.

capability.nextMove: Scale SmCo magnets and Sm metal; qualify with defence and space buyers.
capability.has: IREL's Sm oxide and 3 t/yr SmCo magnet plant (Vizag); BARC and DMRL SmCo technology.

capability.nextMove: No large move: demand has shrunk as LEDs replaced fluorescent lamps. Keep small-scale separation at IREL.
capability.has: IREL lists europium oxide of over 99% purity among its Aluva products. IBM notes that europium is not present in Indian deposits in extractable quantity.

capability.nextMove: Pharma-grade Gd oxide and contrast-agent chemistry.
capability.has: IREL's Gd oxide and BARC's purification; a generic-pharma industry with the chelate chemistry.

capability.nextMove: Downstream: Er-doped fibre and amplifiers for telecom. Buy the oxide (volumes are tiny).
capability.has: CSIR-CGCRI's patented Er-doped and Er/Yb co-doped fibres and EDFA modules, commercialised and available for licensing.

capability.nextMove: Oxide to metal to magnet at scale (the magnet scheme), plus magnet-scrap recycling.
capability.has: IREL's separation (Odisha, Kerala) and Toyotsu's Vizag plant; mini metal plants (La, Ce, Nd) at Bhopal; BARC and DMRL magnet know-how; 20 bidders for the integrated oxide-to-magnet scheme; IREL plans to buy 1,000 t of Nd/NdPr oxide.

capability.nextMove: As neodymium.
capability.has: As neodymium: separated alongside Nd at IREL and Toyotsu.

capability.nextMove: None warranted. If a need arose, production would sit with the atomic-energy establishment's reactors and hot cells.
capability.has: No production. BARC developed promethium-147 sources for a coating-thickness gauge at the Nuclear Fuel Complex in 2009, and its reactors and radiochemistry laboratories make medical isotopes.

capability.nextMove: Buy through partners; no plant is justified.
capability.has: Nothing specific beyond IREL's general separation know-how.

capability.nextMove: Downstream: Yb-doped fibre and fibre lasers; isotope targets.
capability.has: CGCRI's Yb-doped fibres for high-power lasers; BARC's Lu-177 production uses Yb targets.

capability.nextMove: Grow Lu-177 output to replace imports; export once the new reactor runs.
capability.has: BARC/BRIT isotope production in the Dhruva reactor; a dedicated isotope production reactor sanctioned for ~2035.

capability.nextMove: Buy the oxide; explore Tm-doped fibre for lasers.
capability.has: CSIR-CGCRI's doped-fibre know-how (Er, Yb) could extend to Tm.

capability.nextMove: Grow recycling: secure spent catalysts and scrapped converters for Indian refiners, and assess the Boula-Nuasahi deposit.
capability.has: Hindustan Platinum (founded 1961) refines platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium and iridium from spent catalysts and says it is at peak production; Ravindra Heraeus recycles catalysts at Udaipur; Johnson Matthey (Manesar) and BASF (Chennai) coat autocatalysts in India; a Rs 1,500 crore recycling scheme covers catalytic converters. Resources of 20.92 t of platinum-group metals, 67% in Odisha.

ptSteps.label: known elements
ptSteps.caption: Highlighted are the 51 minerals India designates critical. They look like a handful against all 118 known elements. Step through to see how small the pool they are actually drawn from is.

ptSteps.label: occur in nature
ptSteps.caption: Elements 95 to 118 are synthetic, created in particle accelerators and never mined. Set them aside and 94 occur in nature.

ptSteps.label: non-radioactive
ptSteps.caption: Nine more are radioactive with no commercial supply chain, like technetium, polonium and plutonium. That leaves 85.

ptSteps.label: solids & metals
ptSteps.caption: Seven are atmospheric gases such as nitrogen, oxygen and the noble gases, not mined as ores. Down to 78.

ptSteps.label: commercially mined
ptSteps.caption: Set aside hydrogen and helium, and roughly 76 elements are actually mined for commercial use. That is the usable periodic table.

ptSteps.label: designated critical
ptSteps.caption: India designates 51 of these 76 as critical, fully two-thirds. When the label covers that much of what we mine, it can no longer tell policymakers where to act first.

stages.description: Blocks offered or auctioned, exploration licences, offshore and deep-sea areas.
Ore concentration and upgrading (concentrators, mineral separation plants).
Smelting, refining and chemical conversion to metals, oxides and salts.
Battery and advanced materials: cathode, anode, electrolyte, foils, precursors, silicon wafers.
Rare-earth separation, metals and alloys, and permanent magnets.
Battery, e-waste, scrap, catalyst and tailings recovery of canonical minerals.
Centres of Excellence, labs, funded programmes and pilot plants.
Demand anchors: cell gigafactories and compound-semiconductor fabs (off by default).
